newsitem.title: SPAIN: Spanish markets join euphoria over Clinton and EMI report.
newsitem.headline: Spanish markets join euphoria over Clinton and EMI report.

text.p: Spanish bonds hit record highs and the peseta firmed on Wednesday as markets were buoyed by U.S. President Bill Clinton's re-election, but profit-taking cut gains after the release of new European Union forecasts.
Madrid stocks rose to historic peaks, sharing the general euphoria elsewhere in Europe, but shortly afterwards were lagging behind.

Bonds also rose in anticipation of a European Commission report giving economic forecasts for European countries in 1996 and 1997. But gains proved to be short-lived as traders took profits shortly after it was released.

Commenting on the earlier rise in Spanish markets, Jose Luis Alzola, an economist with Salomon Brothers in London, said: "What was a surprise was the speed, because the direction was somehow expected."
A Madrid bond dealer said the market was boosted by the return of "foreign people with big bucks".
"The fact that we are pretty close to the end of the year makes it really good news because it is more likely they have decided to stay at least until 1997," he added.

At 1300 GMT the Ibex index was up 0.8 percent to 4,408.74 and the long-term Spanish bond future contract was trading up 19 basis points to 108.94. It reached a session high of 109.53 percent, compared with the previous October 9 high of 108.42.
The peseta was trading at 84.13 versus the mark, barely changed from 84.135 at Tuesday's close but markedly higher than a week ago.
The spread between 10-year Spanish bonds and their German counterparts stood at 162 basis points, close to historic lows and down from 180 points a week ago and 330 at the beginning of March.
Alzola forecast the spread could drop to 100 basis points within the first half of 1997.
The European Commission on Wednesday forecast that Spanish inflation, as measured by the gross domestic product price deflator, would drop to 2.9 percent in 1997 from 3.6 percent this year.
They also forecast that the public sector deficit as a ratio of gross domestic product should decline in 1997 to 3.0 percent from 4.4 percent in 1996.
Traders said that overall, the Commission's forecasts were generous.
"The European Commission has always kept a positive stance towards a monetary union which is as wide as possible from the start," said Francesco Giordano, economist at San Paolo Bank in London.
With the 1997 budget on its way to final approval, a key factor for Spanish economy will be the inflation trend.

"It's really likely that inflation will break the three percent level in January next year. What is still unclear is if wage inflation will allow the consumer price index to remain under control later on, when the economy picks up," said Alzola.
